docs.title: Daily Practice Checklist
docs.text: Ten minutes a day beats a two-hour workshop once a year. Print this page or pin it.

docs.title: Every day (10 minutes)
docs.text:
• Speak at least once in every meeting
  • Put the main point first in every message
  • Rewrite one message to be shorter before sending
  • Learn & use one phrase from the Phrase Bank
  • One 5-minute AI role-play with the Master Prompt
  • Journal 3 lines: what I said · how it landed · what I'll try next

docs.title: Every week
docs.text:
• Prepare a written 1:1 agenda for your manager
  • Have one conversation outside your team
  • Record yourself for 2 minutes explaining a technical concept
  • Give specific praise to at least two people
  • Try one real-life scenario: order at a café, ask directions, small talk on a train

docs.title: Every month
docs.text:
• Redo the self-assessment
  • Ask for feedback on your communication from one person
  • Do one visibility action: demo, presentation, write-up, knowledge-share
  • Have the one difficult conversation you've been postponing
  • Update your wins file

docs.title: Before any important conversation
docs.text: 1. Goal — what do I want them to know / decide / do? 2. Audience — what do they care about? (altitude rule) 3. Headline — my point in one sentence 4. Evidence — 2–3 facts or numbers 5. Ask — the exact next step 6. Breathe — 4-4-6 breathing, then go

docs.title: Phrase Bank
docs.text:
Learn 5 phrases a week and use each one at least twice in real conversations. Within 3 months you'll have 60 phrases you can say without thinking.

AgreeingDisagreeing politelyAsking for clarityBuying timeOwnershipApologising (when you should)Asking for helpSaying noGiving praiseClosing
  • "That makes sense."
  • "I'm fully on board with that."
  • "Good point. Let's go with it."
  • "I agree, and I'd add one thing…"
  • "I see it a bit differently."
  • "I'm not sure that'll work, because…"
  • "Can I offer another perspective?"
  • "I understand the reasoning. My concern is…"
  • "What if we tried…?"
  • "Could you walk me through that again?"
  • "What do you mean by 'scalable' here?"
  • "Just to make sure I understand: you're saying…?"
  • "Could you give me an example?"
  • "Good question. Let me think about that."
  • "I'd like to check the data before I answer."
  • "Can I get back to you by end of day?"
  • "I'll take care of it."
  • "That's on me. Here's how I'll fix it."
  • "I'll own the follow-up."
  • "You can count on me for this."
  • "I apologise. I missed that."
  • "You're right, I should have flagged it earlier."
  • "Sorry for the confusion. Here's the correct version."

Instead of over-apologising: "Thanks for your patience" · "Thanks for catching that" · "Appreciate you waiting."

  • "Could I get your input on something?"
  • "Do you have 10 minutes to look at this with me?"
  • "I've tried X and Y. What would you suggest next?"
  • "I'd love to help, but I'm at capacity this week."
  • "Not right now. Could we revisit next sprint?"
  • "I can do X, but not Y."
  • "Which should I deprioritise to make room for this?"
  • "Great work on the release. The rollback plan was really thorough."
  • "Thank you, you saved us hours."
  • "I really liked how you explained that to the client."
  • "Let's summarise what we've agreed."
  • "Who's doing what by when?"
  • "I'll send notes shortly."
  • "Thanks, everyone, this was really helpful."

docs.title: Upgrade your vocabulary
docs.text:
Basic Professional "I think" "In my view" / "My recommendation is" "Very important" "Critical" / "High-priority" "Problem" "Issue" / "Challenge" / "Blocker" "Fix" "Resolve" / "Address" "Big" "Significant" / "Substantial" "Check" "Verify" / "Review" "Tell" "Inform" / "Update" / "Flag" "Start" "Kick off" / "Initiate" "Get" "Obtain" / "Receive" "Do the needful" "Please take care of this" / "Could you please [specific action]" "Revert back" "Reply" / "Get back to me" "Prepone" "Move earlier" / "Bring forward" "Kindly do it" "Could you please…" "Same to you" (for "Have a good day") "Thanks, you too!"

Common Indian-English phrases to swap in global teams

"Do the needful", "revert back", "prepone", "out of station", "pass out (graduate)" are understood in India but can confuse global colleagues. Use the professional column above.

docs.title: Day 60 · Client Meetings
docs.text: Day60Phase 4 · Workplace · Day 60 of 80 Done

docs.title: Client Meetings
docs.text: The client is buying confidence as much as software. Prepare well, listen more than you talk, never promise what you can't deliver, and always leave with clear next steps.

docs.title: The client meeting lifecycle
docs.text: 1. Prepare — goal, agenda, attendees, their context, your numbers 2. Open — introductions, agenda, time check 3. Discover / Present — ask questions, then show progress or solution 4. Handle concerns — listen, acknowledge, answer, confirm 5. Close — recap decisions, owners, dates 6. Follow up — minutes within 24 hours

docs.title: Before the meeting: checklist
docs.text:
• Goal: what must be decided or agreed by the end?
  • Agenda sent at least a day in advance
  • Who's attending, and their roles (LinkedIn check)
  • Internal alignment: agree with your manager / account manager on who says what, and what we will not commit to
  • Demo tested on the same network and device you'll use, plus a backup recording
  • Numbers ready: progress %, timelines, open issues
  • Likely questions and your answers (especially about delays and cost)

docs.title: Opening the meeting
docs.text: "Good morning, everyone, and thanks for your time. I'm Ashish, the tech lead for the mobile app. Today we'd like to cover three things: sprint progress, a demo of the new checkout, and two decisions we need from you on payment options. We have 45 minutes. Does that agenda work for you?"

docs.title: Discovery: understand what they need
docs.text:
Question Why "What does success look like for you in 3 months?" Learn their real goal "What's the biggest pain point for your users today?" Find priorities "Who else needs to approve this?" Know the decision-makers "What happens if this launches a month later?" Find out how firm the deadline is "Are there any constraints we should know about: budget, compliance, systems?" Avoid surprises "How do you measure that today?" Get a baseline

Talk 30%, listen 70%

Take notes visibly. Repeat back key points: "So the must-have for launch is UPI and COD. Wallets can come later. Correct?"

docs.title: Scripts for tough moments
docs.text:
Reporting a delayClient asks for something out of scopeYou don't know the answerClient is unhappy / angryClient pushes for an unrealistic deadlineSaying no to a technical demand

"I want to be transparent with you. The payment integration will be 1 week later than planned: the 22nd instead of the 15th. The bank changed their API last week. Everything else is on track. To reduce the impact, we can release the rest of the app on the 15th with COD only. Would that work for you?"

Tell them early, explain the cause in one line, give a new date, and offer an option.

"That's a great idea, and I can see how it helps your sales team. It's outside the current scope, so I don't want to promise it without checking the impact. I'll come back by Thursday with an estimate and options: either adding it as a change request, or swapping it for something lower-priority."

"Good question. I don't want to give you a wrong answer, so let me confirm with our security team and get back to you by tomorrow evening."

"I understand, and I'm sorry this affected your customers during the weekend sale. You're right to be concerned. Here's what happened, what we've already fixed, and what we're changing so it doesn't happen again. I'll personally send you a daily update until it's fully closed."

Don't argue, don't blame the client's team, don't get defensive. Acknowledge, take ownership, give a plan.

"We want to hit that date as much as you do. With the current scope, the earliest high-quality release is the 30th. To launch on the 15th, we could go live with the core ordering flow and add loyalty points two weeks later. Which matters more for your launch: the date or the full feature set?"

"I understand why storing card details looks simpler. We'd recommend against it. It would bring your app under full PCI-DSS compliance, which adds months and cost. Tokenisation via the payment gateway gives you the same user experience with none of that risk."

docs.title: Closing the meeting
docs.text: "Let me quickly recap. Decisions: we launch with UPI and COD; wallets in phase 2. Actions: we share the updated timeline by Wednesday; your team sends the bank sandbox credentials by Friday. Next meeting: Monday at 11. Did I miss anything?"

docs.title: Follow-up email (within 24 hours)
docs.text:
Subject: Minutes — Sprint 6 review | Decisions & next steps

Hi Rohan,

Thanks for your time today. Summary below:

Decisions
• Launch with UPI + COD; wallets moved to phase 2

Action items
• [Us] Updated timeline — Ashish — Wed 6 Nov
• [You] Bank sandbox credentials — Rohan's team — Fri 8 Nov

Open questions
• Data-retention period for order history (awaiting your legal team)

Next meeting: Mon 11 Nov, 11:00 IST

Please let me know if I've missed anything.

Best regards,
Ashish

docs.title: Client etiquette
docs.text: ✅ Do ❌ Don't Join 2–3 minutes early, camera on Argue with your own team in front of the client Use the client's terms ("orders", not "OrderAggregate") Criticise the client's existing systems or vendors Agree internally on who answers what Commit to dates or features without checking Write down every promise you make Discuss internal problems or other clients Say "we", not "they" (for your own company) Use heavy jargon or acronyms without explaining them

docs.title: Beginner vs experienced
docs.text:
BeginnerExperienced
  • You may be there to listen and take notes. Do that brilliantly; it's valued.
  • Speak when asked about your area: short, factual, confident.
  • If unsure whether you can share something, say: "Let me check with Priya and confirm."
  • Pre-wire the meeting: call the client's key person beforehand about anything sensitive.
  • Bring options with trade-offs, not just status.
  • Build the relationship beyond projects: ask about their goals, their pressures, their boss.
  • Protect your team from scope creep, politely and firmly.

docs.title: Day 52 · Day-to-Day Communication
docs.text: Day52Phase 4 · Workplace · Day 52 of 80 Done

docs.title: Day-to-Day Communication
docs.text: People judge you on the small things you do every day: the stand-up, the Slack reply, the PR description. These habits build your reputation faster than one big presentation.

docs.title: Daily stand-up
docs.text:
Format❌ Weak vs ✅ strong 
Yesterday: finished the coupon API, PR #212 in review
Today:     integrate with cart, write tests
Blockers:  need staging DB access — @Ops, can you help after stand-up?

Rules: 30–60 seconds. Outcomes, not activities. Take blockers offline.

❌ Weak ✅ Strong "Yesterday I was working on the bug, still working on it." "The login bug is narrowed to the token refresh. Fix by noon today." "No blockers." (when you're stuck) "I'm stuck on the PDF library. 10 minutes with anyone who's used it?" 5-minute technical deep-dive "Found an interesting caching issue. I'll share in #backend."

docs.title: Golden rules
docs.text:
1. Don't just say "Hi". Write the whole question in one message.
  2. Point first, details after.
  3. Use threads. Don't flood the channel.
  4. Say how urgent it is: "FYI", "When you get a chance", or "Urgent: blocking the release".
  5. Close the loop: "Resolved, thanks!" so nobody else spends time on it.
❌ Instead of ✅ Write "Hi" … (waits 10 min) … "are you there?" "Hi Ravi, quick one: is the orders topic partitioned by customerId or orderId? Writing a consumer and want to keep ordering." "The build is broken" "Main build failing since 11:20 on InventoryIT, looks like a Testcontainers timeout. Looking into it; will update here." "Can we talk?" "Can we talk for 10 min today about the sprint scope? Nothing urgent, just want to align."

docs.title: Email
docs.text:
Subject: [Decision needed by Fri] Choose payment provider for Q1

Hi Priya,

Recommendation: go with Razorpay. Cheaper fees (1.8% vs 2.2%) and the SDK we need.

Options compared: (table / link)
Risk: migration takes ~2 weeks; I've planned it for early Dec.

Could you confirm by Friday so we can start the integration?

Thanks,
Ashish

Tips: the subject line says what you need · the first line gives the answer · under 150 words · one ask · a clear deadline.

docs.title: Pull request descriptions
docs.text:
## What
Adds coupon validation to the checkout flow.

## Why
Expired coupons were being accepted (bug #341), costing ~₹40k/week.

## How
- New `CouponValidator` domain service
- Checks expiry + usage limits before pricing

## Testing
- Unit tests for 6 edge cases
- Manual test on staging with expired coupon ✅

## Risks / Notes for reviewers
Touches the pricing path. Please look closely at `applyDiscount()`.

docs.title: Estimates
docs.text:
• Give ranges, not single numbers: "3 to 5 days".
  • Say what the estimate assumes: "…assuming the API contract doesn't change."
  • Re-estimate out loud when things change: "New info. It's now 7 days, here's why."
  • "I don't know yet. I'll spike for half a day and give you an estimate tomorrow" is a good answer.

docs.title: Useful everyday phrases
docs.text: Situation Say You didn't understand "Sorry, could you say that again? I want to make sure I get it right." Buying time "Good question. Let me check and get back to you by 3." Polite reminder "Gentle nudge on this. Any update?" Saying you're busy "I'm heads-down on the release till 4. Can I look after that?" Agreeing "Makes sense, let's go with that." Partially agreeing "I agree with the approach. One concern about the timeline…" Ending a long call "I think we've covered it. I'll send a summary in 10 minutes." Taking ownership "I'll own this. Expect an update by end of day."

docs.title: Day 61 · Difficult Conversations
docs.text: Day61Phase 4 · Workplace · Day 61 of 80 Done

docs.title: Difficult Conversations
docs.text: The conversation you're avoiding is usually the one you most need to have. Stay calm, be specific, focus on the issue and not the person, and look for what both of you want.

docs.title: The 5-step model
docs.text: 1. Prepare — facts, your goal, their likely view 2. Open safely — "I'd like to talk about X. I want us both to come out of this better." 3. Share facts, then feelings — "When X happened, I felt Y" 4. Listen & understand — "Help me understand your side." 5. Agree on next steps — specific, written, with owners

docs.title: Scripts
docs.text:
Saying noDisagreeing with a seniorConflict with a peerReceiving criticismSomeone takes credit for your workAn angry stakeholder

"I can't take this on this sprint without dropping the payments work. Which should come first?"

Other ways to say no:

  • "Not right now, but I can look at it on Monday."
  • "I'm not the best person for this. Priya knows that system better."
  • "I can do part of it: the API, but not the UI."

"I respect your experience here, so I want to share a different view. I'm worried that skipping integration tests will push bugs into production during the sale. Could we keep tests for the checkout path only? It adds half a day."

"Can we talk about the last few code reviews? I've noticed my PRs sit for 3–4 days, and some comments felt quite harsh. I might be misreading it. How do you see it? I'd like us to work better together."

  1. Breathe. Don't reply instantly.
  2. Thank them: "Thanks for telling me directly."
  3. Clarify: "Can you give me an example?"
  4. Own what's true: "You're right, I missed that."
  5. Commit: "Next time I'll…"

Avoid

"Yes, but…", "That's not fair", or bringing up their mistakes. Even if they're partly wrong, understand first, respond later (you can follow up the next day).

(Privately) "In the demo, the caching work was presented as yours. I built most of it. I'd appreciate it if we credit each other accurately going forward. Can we agree on that?"

(Publicly, at the next chance) "As I mentioned when I built the cache layer…"

"I understand you're frustrated. This outage hurt your customers. Here's what we know, what we're doing, and when you'll hear from me next."

Acknowledge the emotion → give facts → commit to the next update. Don't argue about blame.

docs.title: Phrases that calm things down
docs.text: Instead of Say "You're wrong." "I see it differently." "You always…" "In the last two sprints, I noticed…" "That's not my job." "I can't own that, but let me connect you with someone who can." "Calm down." "I can see this matters a lot. Let's figure it out." "Whatever, fine." "I'm not fully convinced, but I'll commit to it. Let's review in 2 weeks."

docs.title: Practice conversation: Disagreeing with a senior colleague
docs.text: SeniorLet's skip the integration tests this sprint. We don't have time. YouI see why. Can I share a concern? SeniorGo ahead. YouThe sale is next week. Without integration tests on checkout, we could push a bug that costs us orders. SeniorBut the tests take two days. YouWhat if we only test the checkout path? That takes half a day. SeniorOkay, that's a fair compromise. Let's do checkout only. YouThanks. I'll set it up today.

docs.title: Day 56 · Explaining an Issue
docs.text: Day56Phase 4 · Workplace · Day 56 of 80 Done

docs.title: Explaining an Issue
docs.text: A well-explained problem is half-solved. Use these templates for bug reports, incidents, root-cause analysis, and explaining tech to people who aren't technical.

docs.title: The universal structure
docs.text: 1. What's happening — the symptom, in one line 2. Who/what is affected — users, revenue, systems, scale 3. Since when — start time, trigger if known 4. What we know / don't know — facts vs hypotheses 5. What we're doing — actions + owners 6. What's needed + next update — your ask and when you'll report back

docs.title: Templates
docs.text:
Bug report (to a developer)Incident update (Slack / status)Root-cause summary (post-mortem)SBAR (spoken, to a manager) 
**Title:** Cart total ignores coupon when quantity > 10

**Steps to reproduce**
1. Add 11 units of any item
2. Apply coupon SAVE10
3. Go to checkout

**Expected:** Total reduced by 10%
**Actual:** Total unchanged; coupon shows "applied"
**Environment:** staging, build 2026.11.03, Chrome 131
**Evidence:** screenshot + request ID `req-8f2a…`
**Impact:** bulk buyers (≈4% of orders) overpay
**Suspected area:** `PricingService.applyCoupon()` — quantity cap at 10?

🔴 INCIDENT — Checkout errors (SEV-2)
Status: Investigating | Started: 19:10 IST | Next update: 19:40
Impact: ~8% of checkout attempts failing with payment timeout
Known: began after 19:00 payment-SDK deploy
Doing: rolling back SDK (owner: Ravi), monitoring error rate (owner: Meena)
Need: nothing yet

Then keep updating on schedule, even if there's no news: "No change. Rollback 60% complete. Next update 20:00."

## Summary
Checkout failed for 40 min (19:10–19:50) — ~1,200 orders affected.

## Timeline
19:00 deploy · 19:10 alerts · 19:18 incident declared · 19:35 rollback · 19:50 recovered

## Root cause
New SDK default timeout (2 s) was lower than our bank's p95 (2.6 s) under load.

## What went well / what didn't
+ Alerting fired within 2 min
− Deploy happened at peak time; no canary

## Action items
| Action | Owner | Due |
|---|---|---|
| Canary deploys for payment service | Ravi | 15 Nov |
| Block peak-hour deploys in CI | Meena | 10 Nov |

Blameless language

Write "The deploy pipeline allowed a peak-hour release", not "Ravi deployed at peak time". Fix the system, not the person.

Situation: "Order emails aren't being sent." Background: "Since 10 am, after the email provider rotated our API key." Assessment: "About 3,000 customers haven't got confirmations. No orders are lost." Recommendation: "I've requested a new key; ETA 30 min. Meanwhile, should support post a banner?"

docs.title: Explaining tech to non-tech people
docs.text:
Use one analogy + one number + one action.

Concept Analogy Cache "A sticky note on your desk, so you don't walk to the filing cabinet every time." Database index "The index at the back of a book. Without it, you read every page." Load balancer "A restaurant host seating guests across all the waiters, not just one." Message queue (Kafka) "A post office. Senders drop letters; receivers collect them at their own pace." Tech debt "Skipping car servicing. Fine for a while, then a big expensive breakdown." Microservices "Separate shops in a mall instead of one giant store. One can close for repairs without shutting the mall." API "A waiter: you order from the menu; you don't walk into the kitchen." Encryption "A locked box only the receiver has the key to." Race condition "Two people booking the last train seat at the same second."

Putting it together

"The site was slow because our 'sticky note' (cache) got wiped during the update, so every page went to the 'filing cabinet' (database). Pages took 6 seconds instead of 1. We've refilled it, and we're adding a check so updates don't wipe it again."

docs.title: Mistakes when explaining issues
docs.text:
• ❌ "It's broken" (what is? for whom? since when?)
  • ❌ Mixing guesses with facts. Say "We know…" and "We suspect…"
  • ❌ Going silent during an incident. Silence feels worse than bad news.
  • ❌ Blaming a person or team in public
  • ❌ Too much detail for the audience (see altitude rule)

docs.title: Practice conversation: Explaining an outage to a non-tech manager
docs.text: ManagerCustomers say the app was slow this morning. What happened? YouBetween 9 and 9:40, pages took six seconds to load instead of one. About 15% of users were affected. ManagerWhy? YouOur cache, which is like a sticky note so we don't go to the filing cabinet every time, was cleared during an update. ManagerIs it fixed? YouYes. We refilled the cache at 9:40, and everything is normal now. ManagerWill it happen again? YouWe're adding a check so updates can't clear the cache. It'll be done by Friday.

docs.title: Day 62 · Global & Remote Teams
docs.text: Day62Phase 4 · Workplace · Day 62 of 80 Done

docs.title: Global & Remote Teams
docs.text: When your team spans time zones and cultures, writing well matters more than talking well. Be explicit, write things down, be clear about time zones, and don't assume others share your context.

docs.title: Principles
docs.text:
• Write it down

    Decisions, context and next steps go in writing. Remote teams run on docs, not hallway chats.

  • Respect time zones

    Always state time zones. Rotate meeting times so the same people aren't always up late.

  • Over-communicate

    No one can see you working. Post progress, blockers and status changes.

  • Explicit > implicit

    Say "Yes, I'll do it by Thursday" rather than "I'll try". Avoid idioms and local slang.

docs.title: Cultural communication styles
docs.text:
Style Some cultures tend to… Tips Direct vs indirect US / Netherlands / Germany: direct "No, that won't work" · India / Japan: softer "That may be difficult" Learn to read both. If unsure, ask: "Just to confirm, is that a no?" Yes means… In India, "yes" can mean "I heard you", not "I agree / I can" Say what you mean: "Yes, done by Friday" or "I can't commit to Friday; Monday is realistic." Hierarchy Some teams expect juniors to wait to be asked; others expect everyone to challenge In global teams, speaking up and disagreeing politely is expected, including with seniors Small talk US: short, friendly · Europe: varies · India: personal questions are normal Avoid salary, age, marriage questions with global colleagues Time Some cultures treat meeting start times as exact Join on time; 2 minutes late is late

The 'yes' trap

When a client asks "Can you deliver by Friday?" and the honest answer is "probably not", saying "yes" to be polite causes a much bigger problem on Friday. A clear "no, but…" builds more trust: "Friday is too tight for full testing. Tuesday is realistic. Or we ship on Friday without the export feature."

docs.title: Async communication
docs.text:
Good async messageHandoff across time zonesRecording instead of meeting 
Context: Cart API p95 jumped to 1.2 s after yesterday's deploy (graph attached).
What I found: new N+1 query in getCartItems() — PR #251 fixes it.
Need from you: review PR #251 by your EOD (Thu, 6 pm CET).
If no reply: I'll merge with Meena's review at 10:00 IST Fri.

Context → finding → ask → deadline (with time zone) → default action.

🌅 End-of-day handoff (IST → US team)
Done: payment retries merged & deployed to staging
In progress: refund webhook — 70%, branch feat/refund-webhook
Blocked: need Stripe test keys — @Mike can you share?
Watch out: staging DB restarts at 02:00 UTC (maintenance)

For demos and walkthroughs, record a 5-minute Loom-style video plus a written summary. It saves a meeting at 10 pm for someone.

docs.title: Meetings across time zones
docs.text:
• Always write times with zone: "Thu 4:30 pm IST / 12 pm CET / 6 am ET"
  • Prefer the overlap window; rotate inconvenient slots
  • Share an agenda and doc beforehand so non-native speakers can prepare
  • Summarise in writing afterwards; not everyone catches everything on a call
  • Speak slowly and clearly; avoid idioms ("ballpark", "touch base", "low-hanging fruit") with mixed audiences, or explain them

docs.title: Accents and understanding each other
docs.text: Situation Say You didn't catch something "Sorry, the audio cut out for me. Could you repeat the last part?" Still didn't get it "Could you type that in the chat? I want to get it exactly right." Confirm understanding "So you need the API by Tuesday your time, correct?" They didn't understand you Rephrase with simpler words, don't just repeat louder Speaking fast from nerves Slow down; pause between points; use the chat for numbers/names

docs.title: Common Indian-English phrases in global teams
docs.text:
Phrase Global colleagues may hear Use instead "Do the needful" Unclear request "Could you please approve the PR?" "I have a doubt" "I disagree / don't believe it" "I have a question" "Revert back" "Undo a change" "Reply" / "Get back to me" "Prepone" Unknown word "Move earlier" "Kindly adjust" Confusing "Could you please…" "Out of station" Unclear "Travelling" / "Out of town" "Today itself" Unusual phrasing "Today" / "By end of today"

See the full list in the Phrase Bank.

docs.text: MikeCan you get the fix in before our morning? YouJust to confirm, your morning is 9 am Eastern time, which is 7:30 pm here in India. Is that right? MikeYes, exactly. YouThen yes, I'll have it merged by 6 pm IST, so it's on staging before you start. MikeGreat. And if something goes wrong? YouI'll post an update in the channel by 6:30 pm IST either way, with the status and next steps. MikePerfect, thanks.

docs.title: Day 64 · Leave & Boundaries
docs.text: Day64Phase 4 · Workplace · Day 64 of 80 Done

docs.title: Asking for Leave & Setting Boundaries
docs.text: Rested engineers write better code. Asking for leave and protecting your time are part of being a professional. Plan ahead, cover your work, and say it clearly without guilt.

docs.title: Asking for planned leave
docs.text:
1. Check — team calendar, release dates, on-call rota 2. Ask early — 2–4 weeks ahead for a week off; more for long leave 3. Plan cover — who handles what while you're away 4. Confirm in writing — leave system + calendar + team channel 5. Hand over — notes before you go; out-of-office on Asking your managerSick leave (same day)Emergency leaveLong leave (wedding, parental, medical)

"I'd like to take leave from 15th to 22nd December for a family trip. I've checked: it's after the release, and Ravi can cover my on-call shift. I'll finish the search work and hand over notes before I go. Does that work for you?"

Note the wording: "I'd like to take", not "Can I please, if it's okay, maybe…"

Hi Priya, I'm unwell today (fever) and won't be able to work. I'll take sick leave.
Urgent items: PR #231 needs a review — Meena, could you take it?
I'll update you tomorrow morning.

Short and clear. You don't need to give medical details.

Hi Priya, I have a family emergency and need to leave right away. I'll be offline for
the rest of today, possibly tomorrow. Ravi has context on the cart bug.
I'll update you as soon as I can.

"I wanted to give you early notice: I'm planning parental leave from March for 3 months. I'd like to plan the handover together. Could we put together a coverage plan over the next few weeks?"

docs.title: Out-of-office message
docs.text:
Thanks for your message. I'm on leave from 15–22 Dec with limited access to email.
For urgent checkout issues, please contact Ravi Kumar (ravi@example.com).
For everything else, I'll reply after I return on 23 Dec.

docs.title: Handover note before leave
docs.text:
Leave handover — Ashish (15–22 Dec)
• Search filters: merged; feature flag OFF — Meena to enable after QA sign-off
• Bug #341: root cause found, fix in PR #245 — needs one more review
• On-call: swapped with Ravi (15–18 Dec)
• Don't panic if: nightly report job warns about latency — known issue, ticket #350

docs.title: Saying no to after-hours work (politely)
docs.text:
Late-evening requestWeekend messagesToo many meetingsBeing pulled into everything

"I'm logging off for the day. I'll pick this up first thing at 9:30 tomorrow. If it's a production issue, the on-call engineer is Meena."

(Monday) "Saw your weekend message. I'll have it done by noon today. Going forward, if something is urgent on a weekend, a call is the best way to reach me, so I don't miss it, and I can switch off when it's not."

"I'm in meetings 5–6 hours a day, and coding work is slipping. Could I block 10 am–1 pm as focus time, and drop the meetings where I'm optional?"

"I'm happy to help, but if I take this, the search release slips. Can we check with Priya which one is the priority?"

docs.title: Boundary habits
docs.text:
• Set working hours in Slack/Teams and calendar
  • Turn off notifications after hours (except on-call)
  • Schedule-send late-night messages for the morning so others don't feel pressure
  • Block focus time on your calendar, and protect it
  • Say "Let me check my calendar" before agreeing to anything big

Boundaries for leads

Your behaviour sets the norm. If you message at midnight, your team thinks they must answer at midnight. Use schedule-send, and take your own leave visibly.

Ravi has agreed to cover my on-call shift. ManagerWhat about the search work? YouI'll finish it before I go and write a handover note. ManagerSounds good. Approved. Enjoy your trip! YouThank you!

docs.title: Day 57 · Meetings & Presentations
docs.text: Day57Phase 4 · Workplace · Day 57 of 80 Done

docs.title: Meetings & Presentations
docs.text: If you don't speak in meetings, people won't know what you know. Speaking up is part of the job, and so is running a meeting well and giving a demo people remember.

docs.title: How to speak up (when you find it hard)
docs.text:
• Prepare one point

    Read the agenda beforehand and write one question or opinion.

  • Speak early

    The first 5 minutes are the easiest. Waiting makes it harder.

  • Build on others

    "Adding to what Meena said…" is a low-risk way in.

  • Ask a question

    A good question counts as a contribution: "How will we measure success?"

docs.title: Phrases to enter a conversation
docs.text:
• "Can I add something here?"
  • "Building on that point…"
  • "I have a slightly different view."
  • "Before we move on, can I raise one risk?"
  • "Sorry to interrupt. Quick clarification:"

docs.title: When someone interrupts you
docs.text: "Sorry, Rahul, let me just finish this point, then I'd love to hear yours."

docs.title: Running a meeting
docs.text:
• Purpose in the invite: "Decide on X" or "Review Y" (not "Discuss")
  • Agenda with time boxes
  • Only the people needed to make the decision
  • Start on time; recap the goal in the first minute
  • Park off-topic items: "Great point. Let's take that offline."
  • End 5 minutes early with decisions + owners + dates
  • Send notes within an hour

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
1. Hook (30 s): the problem, in the user's words. "Customers kept asking: where's my order?"
  2. Show (most of the time): the live demo, following the happy path
  3. Impact: numbers, or what's now possible
  4. Next steps / asks
  5. Q&A

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Rehearse twice out loud. Once alone, once with a friend or AI.
  • Have a backup: screenshots or a recording in case the demo breaks.
  • Increase font size (Ctrl/Cmd +) and close Slack and email notifications.
  • One message per slide. Slide titles should be sentences: "Search is 3× faster", not "Results".
  • Pause after key points. Silence makes them stick.

docs.title: Handling Q&A
docs.text: Situation Response Good question you can answer Answer in 1–3 sentences, then "Does that answer it?" You don't know "I don't know, but I'll find out and send it to everyone by tomorrow." Hostile question "That's a fair concern." Then answer calmly, with facts. Off-topic "Great question. Can we take that offline after this?" Long rambling question "If I understand, you're asking about X. Is that right?"

docs.title: Video call etiquette
docs.text:
• Camera on for 1:1s and small meetings
  • Mute when not speaking; unmute before you start talking
  • Look at the camera, not the screen, when making your main point
  • Use the chat for links, not side conversations
  • Say your name before speaking in large calls: "Ashish here. Quick question."

docs.title: Practice conversation: Handling a tough question in a demo
docs.text: DirectorThis looks good, but what happens if the payment gateway goes down during a sale? YouThat's a fair concern. We retry three times, and then we switch to a backup gateway automatically. DirectorHow long does the switch take? YouUnder five seconds. Customers don't see an error. DirectorHave you tested it? YouYes, we tested it last week with fake failures. I can share the results after the meeting. DirectorPlease do.

docs.title: Day 65 · Mentoring
docs.text: Day65Phase 4 · Workplace · Day 65 of 80 Done

docs.title: Mentoring
docs.text:
Mentoring is one of the fastest ways to grow, whichever side you're on. A good mentee asks better questions, and a good mentor learns to explain clearly, listen properly, and let other people succeed. This page covers both sides.

Related pages

Talking to Juniors covers day-to-day teaching and code-review feedback. This page is about structured, longer-term mentoring relationships, inside or outside your team.

docs.title: Mentor, coach, sponsor: what's the difference?
docs.text:
Role What they do Example Mentor Shares experience and advice "When I moved to tech lead, here's what I wish I'd known…" Coach Asks questions so you find the answer "What options do you see? What's stopping you?" Sponsor Uses their influence for you when you're not in the room "Kavya should lead the new project. She's ready." Buddy Helps a new joiner settle in "Here's how deploys work; let's grab lunch."

Good mentors move between all of these as needed.

1. Agree — goals, frequency, how you'll communicate 2. Meet regularly — 30–45 minutes, every 2–4 weeks 3. Act — the mentee tries things between sessions 4. Reflect — what worked, what didn't, what's next 5. Review & close — after 3–6 months, celebrate and decide whether to continue Being a mentee Being a mentor

docs.title: Finding a mentor
docs.text:
Look for someone 1–2 steps ahead of you on the path you want, not necessarily the most senior person you know. Look at your company's other teams, ex-colleagues, meetups and communities.

"Hi Meena, I really liked your talk on event-driven design. I'm working towards a senior backend role, and I'd value your perspective. Would you be open to a 30-minute chat once a month for the next 3 months? I'll come prepared with specific questions, and I'm happy to work around your schedule."

Why this works: it's specific about why you chose them, it has a clear goal, the time ask is limited, and you've shown you'll make it easy for them.

Start small

Don't open with "Will you be my mentor?" That feels like a big commitment. Ask for one conversation about a specific topic. If it goes well, ask for another.

docs.title: Preparing for each session
docs.text:
Mentoring session — [Date]
Since last time: led my first design review (went OK; lost control of the discussion)
Question 1: how do you keep a design review on track when two seniors argue?
Question 2: should I learn Kubernetes deeply or stay focused on backend?
Want feedback on: my design doc for the slot service (link)

docs.title: Questions worth asking a mentor
docs.text:
• "What do you wish you'd known at my stage?"
  • "What separates good engineers from great ones, in your experience?"
  • "How did you handle [specific situation]?"
  • "What would you do in my position?"
  • "What am I not asking that I should be?"
  • "Can you review this doc / code / talk and be honest?"

docs.title: Being a good mentee
docs.text:
• ✅ Own the relationship: schedule the sessions, send the agenda, follow up
  • ✅ Try their advice and report back: "I tried your suggestion; here's what happened"
  • ✅ Respect their time: finish on time; cancel early if you must
  • ✅ Say thank you specifically: "Your advice on design reviews really helped me last week."
  • ❌ Expecting them to solve your problems or get you promoted
  • ❌ Only getting in touch when you need something

docs.title: Ending gracefully
docs.text: "These last six months have been really valuable. I've led three design reviews and I'm much more confident. Thank you. I'd love to stay in touch, and I'll let you know how the promotion cycle goes."

docs.title: The first session
docs.text:
"Let's start with what you want from this. Where would you like to be in 6 months, and what's getting in the way right now? Also, how do you like to get feedback: direct, or gentler?"

Agree on:

  • Goals: 1–3 specific outcomes (e.g. "lead a design review", "get promoted to SDE-2")
  • Rhythm: how often, how long, video or in person
  • Confidentiality: what's said stays between you
  • Honesty: "I'll be direct with you; tell me if something isn't helping."

docs.title: Listen more, advise less (the GROW model)
docs.text:
Step Question Goal "What do you want to get out of today's conversation?" Reality "What's happening right now? What have you tried?" Options "What could you do? What else?" Way forward "What will you do, and by when?"

Ask before telling. Give your own advice only after they've thought it through. Then share it as a story: "When I faced this, here's what I did, and here's what I'd do differently."

docs.title: Useful mentor phrases
docs.text: Situation Say They want the answer "I'll share my view, but first, what's your instinct?" They're too hard on themselves "What would you tell a friend in this situation?" They're avoiding something "I notice we keep coming back to this. What makes it hard?" Giving hard feedback "Can I share something that might be uncomfortable to hear?" They succeeded "That's a real step up. What did you do differently this time?" You don't know "I haven't faced that one. Let me introduce you to someone who has."

docs.title: Go beyond advice
docs.text:
• Open doors: introduce them to people they should know.
  • Give visibility: "Would you like to present this at the architecture review?"
  • Sponsor: speak their name in rooms they aren't in.
  • Share your mistakes: your failures teach more than your successes.

docs.title: Mentor mistakes
docs.text:
• ❌ Turning every session into stories about yourself
  • ❌ Creating a mini-me: their path doesn't have to be yours
  • ❌ Solving their problems for them (they learn nothing)
  • ❌ Breaking confidence, even casually
  • ❌ Cancelling repeatedly; it signals they aren't a priority

You're never too junior to mentor

A 2-year engineer can mentor an intern, and a junior can reverse-mentor a senior on new tools, AI workflows, or what new joiners find confusing.

docs.title: Group & peer mentoring
docs.text:
• Peer circles: 4–6 people at the same level meet monthly and each brings one challenge.
  • Mentoring office hours: a senior engineer holds an open hour every week; anyone can drop in.
  • Book / paper club: read one chapter or article, discuss how it applies to your work.
  • Communities: meetups, open source, online forums. Mentors don't have to be at your company.

docs.title: Practice conversation: First conversation with a mentor
docs.text: YouThank you for agreeing to mentor me. I know you're busy. MentorHappy to. What would you like to get out of this? YouI want to grow into a senior role in the next year. I think my weak area is leading design discussions. MentorWhat happens in design discussions now? YouI usually have ideas, but I don't speak until the end, and then the decision is already made. MentorThat's common. What if, in your next design review, you share your view in the first ten minutes? YouThat's scary, but I'll try. Can we meet again in two weeks to talk about how it went? MentorSure. Send me the date of the review.

docs.title: Day 67 · Office Party & Team Events
docs.text: Day67Phase 4 · Workplace · Day 67 of 80 Done

docs.title: Office Party & Team Events
docs.text: An office party is still work, just more relaxed. People remember how you made them feel, not what you said about Kafka. Turn up, mix with people, be warm, and leave on a good note.

docs.title: The party game plan
docs.text: 1. Arrive — within the first 30 minutes, when groups are still forming 2. Greet — your manager / host first, then your team 3. Mix — talk to 3 people outside your usual circle 4. Enjoy — join the games, food, photos; don't hide behind your phone 5. Exit — thank the organisers and leave while you're still fresh

docs.title: Openers that always work
docs.text:
With colleagues you barely knowWith senior leadersAbout the event itselfPersonal (safe) topics
  • "Hi, I'm Ashish from the checkout team. I don't think we've properly met!"
  • "How long have you been with the company?"
  • "Which team are you on? What are you working on these days?"
  • "Hi Ma'am / Sir, I'm Ashish, I work on the delivery-tracking feature. Great event, thanks for organising it."
  • "What's been the highlight of the year for you?"
  • "Is there anything you're excited about for next year?"

Tip

Keep it short (2–3 minutes). Leaders want to meet many people. Don't pitch projects or ask for a promotion at a party.

  • "The food's great. Have you tried the biryani?"
  • "Are you joining the quiz? We need one more for our team."
  • "Who organised this? They did a great job."
  • "Any plans for the holidays?"
  • "Have you watched anything good lately?"
  • "Where are you from originally?"
  • "Do you do anything fun on weekends? Sports, music?"

docs.title: Joining and leaving groups
docs.text: Situation Say / do Join a group Stand at the edge, smile, wait for a pause: "Mind if I join you?" Bring someone in "Priya, have you met Arjun? He's the one who built the new search." Leave a conversation "Great chatting! I'm going to grab some food. Catch you later." Leave the party "Thanks so much for organising, I had a great time. See you Monday!"

docs.title: Toasts, speeches & awards
docs.text:
Giving a short toastReceiving an awardAsked to say something unexpectedly

"Can I have everyone's attention for one minute? This year we launched 3 cities and survived two sale days without downtime, and that's because of everyone in this room. Special thanks to the platform team for the late nights. To an even better next year. Cheers!"

Under 60 seconds · one specific achievement · thank people by name · end with a cheer.

"Thank you, I'm honestly surprised! This was a team effort. Meena, Ravi and Kavya did the heavy lifting on the migration. Thank you all."

"I wasn't expecting this! I'll just say: I've learned more this year than in the last three, thanks to this team. Thank you!"

docs.title: Etiquette: do's and don'ts
docs.text:
✅ Do ❌ Don't Dress one step smarter than the dress code Drink too much; know your limit (or stick to mocktails) Put your phone away Talk about work problems, salaries or appraisals Talk to new joiners and quiet people Gossip or complain about colleagues or managers Take part in games, even if you're bad at them Stay only with your own team all evening Thank the organisers Make jokes about religion, politics, appearance Respect people who don't drink or eat certain food Pressure anyone to drink, dance or "loosen up"

The next-morning test

Before you say or post something, ask: "Would I be comfortable if my manager and HR heard this on Monday?" Party photos and videos travel fast.

docs.title: For introverts
docs.text:
• Set a goal: 3 meaningful conversations, then you're allowed to leave.
  • Volunteer to help organise. It gives you a role and natural reasons to talk.
  • Arrive early. Small groups are easier than a full room.
  • Stand near the food or drinks. People come to you.
  • Ask questions and let others talk. Good listeners are always welcome.

docs.title: For seniors & managers
docs.text:
• Go round every table, especially to people who don't normally see you.
  • Thank people publicly for specific work.
  • Make sure new joiners are included.
  • Leave a little early so the team can relax, and settle any team bill quietly.

docs.title: Practice conversation: Meeting a senior leader at a party
docs.text: YouHi, I'm Ashish from the checkout team. Great event, thanks for organising it. VPHi Ashish! Glad you're enjoying it. What do you work on? YouThe delivery-slot feature. We launched it in three new cities this year. VPOh, that was your team? That was a big win. YouThank you. It was a real team effort. What's been the highlight of the year for you? VPHonestly, seeing the team grow. We hired forty people this year. YouThat's amazing. Well, I won't keep you. Enjoy the evening! VPYou too. Nice meeting you, Ashish.

docs.title: Day 54 · Peers & Cross-Team
docs.text: Day54Phase 4 · Workplace · Day 54 of 80 Done

docs.title: Peers & Cross-Team Communication
docs.text: Most of the time you have influence but no authority. You can't order the product manager, the QA lead or another team around. You persuade them by building a relationship and making your ask easy to say yes to.

docs.title: Know what each role cares about
docs.text: Role Cares about Speak their language Product Manager User value, scope, dates "This lets users do X; trade-off is Y." Designer User experience, consistency "This interaction is expensive. Could a simpler pattern work?" QA Coverage, edge cases, stability "Here are the risky areas to test first." DevOps / SRE Reliability, on-call pain "Here's the runbook and the alerts." Other dev team Their own roadmap, API stability "Here's the contract change, and here's the migration window." Sales / Support Customer promises "This ships on the 15th; here's what to tell customers."

docs.title: Scripts
docs.text:
Asking another team for somethingNegotiating scope with a PMDisagreeing in a design reviewFollowing up when they've gone silentThanking publicly

"Hi Neha, I'm on the checkout team. We need a new reserveStock endpoint by the 20th to launch flash sales. I've drafted the API contract (link). Could your team review it this week? If it helps, we can raise the PR ourselves and you just review."

"I love this feature. In the 2 weeks we have, we can deliver filters and sorting, but not saved searches. Which matters more for the launch? We can add saved searches in the next sprint."

"I see the benefit of event sourcing here. My concern is the extra complexity for a team of three. What if we start with a simple outbox table and move to event sourcing if audit needs grow? Happy to be convinced otherwise."

"Hi Arjun, following up on the contract review from Monday. We need it by Thursday to keep the launch date. If you're swamped, a 10-minute call might be faster. Does tomorrow at 11 work?"

"Big thanks to @Kavya from the platform team. She stayed late to fix the Kafka config so we could release on time. 🙏"

docs.title: Building cross-team relationships
docs.text:
• Coffee chats: 20 minutes with one person from another team each month.
  • Help first: review their PR or answer their question before you need something from them.
  • Close the loop: tell people what happened with their input ("We used your idea, and it worked").
  • Assume good intent: a slow reply usually means they're busy, not that they don't care.

docs.title: Practice conversation: Asking another team for help
docs.text: YouHi Neha, I'm Ashish from the checkout team. Do you have a minute? NehaSure, what's up? YouWe need a new stock-reservation endpoint for the flash sale on the 20th. I've drafted the API contract. NehaThe 20th is tight for us. We're busy with the warehouse migration. YouI understand. Would it help if we wrote the code and your team only reviewed it? NehaThat would help a lot. Send me the contract and I'll review it by Thursday. YouPerfect. Thank you, Neha.

docs.title: Day 59 · Talking to the CEO
docs.text: Day59Phase 4 · Workplace · Day 59 of 80 Done

docs.title: Talking to the CEO & Executives
docs.text: Executives have 30 seconds of attention for your topic and 100 other problems waiting. Lead with the answer, translate tech into business, and make the decision easy for them.

docs.title: What executives care about
docs.text:
• Money

    Revenue, cost, ROI. "This saves ₹12 lakh a year in cloud spend."

  • Customers

    Experience, churn, NPS. "Checkout failures dropped 60%."

  • Risk

    Security, compliance, outages, reputation.

  • Speed

    Time-to-market, competitive edge.

docs.title: The executive formula
docs.text: 1. Headline — the answer or the ask in one sentence 2. Impact — money, customers, risk, in numbers 3. Options — 2 or 3, with your recommendation 4. Ask — the exact decision you need, and by when

docs.title: Translate tech into business
docs.text: Engineer says CEO hears Say instead "We need to refactor the monolith." "Engineers want to play with code." "Every new feature takes 3 weeks instead of 1. Splitting the system doubles our release speed." "We have tech debt." "Vague complaint." "Fixing 3 fragile areas cuts outages by about half, and each outage costs us ~₹4 lakh." "p99 latency is 3 seconds." "?" "1 in 100 customers waits 3 seconds at checkout, and 20% of those abandon." "We need Kubernetes." "Expensive buzzword." "We can handle sale-day traffic without manual work, and stop over-paying for idle servers." "The DB is a single point of failure." "?" "If one server dies, the whole site is down for hours. A backup costs ₹30k/month."

docs.title: Scripts
docs.text:
30-second elevator updateExplaining an outageAsking for budget / headcountAnswering \"Why is this late?\"When you don't know the answer

"The new delivery-tracking feature launches Monday. Early tests show 25% fewer 'where is my order' calls. One risk: map API costs may rise 15%, and we have a fallback ready. No decision needed today."

"Yesterday, checkout was down for 40 minutes, from 7:10 to 7:50 pm. About 1,200 orders failed, roughly ₹9 lakh in sales. Cause: a database update ran during peak hours. We've recovered, and 70% of affected customers have already re-ordered after our coupon email. To prevent repeats, all DB changes now go through an automated check and run only off-peak. I'd like approval for 2 sprints of reliability work. Can I count on that?"

"I'm asking for 2 more backend engineers for Q1. Right now the team spends 40% of its time on support tickets, so the loyalty program slips to Q3. With 2 hires, it ships in Q2, which product estimates adds ₹1.5 crore in annual repeat revenue. Cost is about ₹60 lakh a year. Can we approve this by the 15th so we can start hiring?"

"It's 2 weeks late because the payment partner changed their API mid-project. We've finished the rework, and the new date is the 22nd, with high confidence. Going forward, we're adding partner-change checks to our planning."

No blame, no long story. Cause, new date, and the fix for next time.

"I don't have that number right now. I'll get it to you by 3 pm today."

Never guess numbers in front of executives.

docs.title: Before you walk in: checklist
docs.text:
• Can I say my main point in one sentence?
  • Do I have numbers (₹, %, users, hours)?
  • Do I have 2–3 options and a recommendation?
  • Do I know the exact decision I'm asking for?
  • Have I pre-wired it with my manager and other key people?
  • Is there a 1-page summary I can leave behind?
  • Have I prepared answers for "What if we do nothing?" and "What's the risk?"

docs.title: Mistakes to avoid
docs.text:
• ❌ Starting with background ("So, in 2023 we chose MongoDB because…")
  • ❌ Jargon without translation
  • ❌ Showing 30 slides when 3 will do
  • ❌ Surprising your manager by going over their head
  • ❌ Getting defensive when interrupted. Interruptions are normal. Answer and move on.

docs.title: For experienced engineers
docs.text:
• Learn the company's top 3 goals this year and tie every proposal to one of them.
  • Say less. "Yes, it's on track" is a complete answer if that's what was asked.
  • Build relationships before you need them: a coffee chat with a VP is worth more than a slide deck.
  • Bring the "so what" for the business, not just the technical "what".

docs.title: Practice conversation: The 30-second update in a corridor
docs.text: CEOAshish, right? How's the delivery tracking project? YouIt launches on Monday. In testing, "where is my order" calls dropped by 25%. CEOExcellent. Any risks? YouOne: map costs may go up about 15%. We already have a cheaper backup provider ready. CEOGood. Anything you need from me? YouNo decision needed today. I'll share the launch results next Friday. CEOGreat work. Keep me posted.

docs.title: Day 55 · Talking to Juniors
docs.text: Day55Phase 4 · Workplace · Day 55 of 80 Done

docs.title: Talking to Juniors
docs.text: Your job isn't to be the smartest person in the room. It's to make the room smarter. How you treat juniors decides whether they come to you with problems or hide them from you.

docs.title: Principles
docs.text:
1. Psychological safety first. Juniors who are scared to ask hide bugs.
  2. Explain the why, not just the what. "Use a transaction here because two writes must succeed together."
  3. Ask before telling. "What do you think is happening?" builds thinking. Giving the answer builds dependence.
  4. Praise in public, correct in private.
  5. Be specific. "Good job" teaches nothing. "Your test for the null-cart case caught a real bug, nice" does.

docs.title: Teaching: the "I do, we do, you do" model
docs.text: I do — you demo while explaining your thinking out loud We do — pair programming; they drive, you guide You do — they do it alone; you review afterward

docs.title: Scripts
docs.text:
Onboarding a new juniorCode-review feedbackFeedback on a bigger problemDelegating a taskWhen they're stuck but won't askWhen they make a mistakeSaying no to their idea (kindly)

"Welcome! For the first two weeks, nobody expects you to ship big features. Your only job is to learn and ask questions. There are no stupid ones here. Let's do 15 minutes every day at 4 pm for whatever came up."

Use labels so they know how serious each comment is:

nit:        (optional, style) "nit: could rename `d` to `deliveryDate` for clarity."
suggestion: (better approach)  "suggestion: a Map lookup would make this O(1) instead of O(n)."
question:   (curious, not a demand) "question: what happens if the list is empty?"
blocker:    (must fix) "blocker: this SQL is built by string concat — injection risk. Use a parameter."
praise:     "praise: really clean separation of the domain logic here 👏"

Use SBI: Situation → Behaviour → Impact → (then ask)

"In yesterday's release (situation), the PR was merged without tests (behaviour). A bug reached production and took 2 hours to roll back (impact). What got in the way of adding tests? How can I help next time?"

"I'd like you to own the coupon-validation endpoint. Goal: reject expired and over-used coupons. Done means: endpoint + unit tests + docs. Deadline: Thursday. Check-in: let's sync Tuesday. You decide the design; I'm here if you get stuck."

"Hey, how's the migration going? Getting stuck is completely normal on this one. It took me two days the first time. Want to walk me through where you are?"

"This happens to everyone. I once took down staging for a whole afternoon. Let's fix it together first, then talk about how to prevent it."

"I like that you're thinking about performance. Right now, the bottleneck is the database, not the JSON parsing, so a rewrite wouldn't help much. Can you profile it and show me where the time goes? If the data says otherwise, let's do it."

docs.title: Mistakes to avoid
docs.text:
• ❌ "This is easy, just do X" (it isn't easy for them)
  • ❌ Taking the keyboard and fixing it yourself
  • ❌ Sarcasm in code reviews
  • ❌ Only giving feedback when something goes wrong
  • ❌ Answering in jargon without checking they understand

docs.title: Questions to ask juniors regularly
docs.text:
• "What's one thing you learned this week?"
  • "What's confusing about our codebase that nobody explains?"
  • "What would you like to work on next?"
  • "How can I be a better mentor for you?"

docs.title: Practice conversation: Feedback on a junior's PR
docs.text: YouHi Kavya, I've reviewed your PR. Have you got ten minutes? KavyaYes. Is it bad? YouNot at all. The logic is clean and easy to read. There are two things to fix before we merge. KavyaOkay. YouFirst, there are no tests for the empty-cart case. What do you think happens if the cart is empty? KavyaOh… it might throw an error. YouExactly. And second, the SQL is built with string concatenation. Can you use a parameter instead? KavyaYes, I'll fix both today. YouGreat. Ping me when it's ready, and I'll approve it quickly.

docs.title: Day 53 · Talking to Your Manager
docs.text: Day53Phase 4 · Workplace · Day 53 of 80 Done

docs.title: Talking to Your Manager
docs.text: Your manager's three wishes: no surprises, clear status, and problems that arrive with options. Give them those three things and they'll trust you.

docs.title: What your manager actually needs
docs.text: They need So you should Predictability Share status before they ask Early warning Raise risks the moment you see them, not on deadline day Options, not just problems Bring 2 possible solutions with every problem Something to tell their boss Summarise in 1–2 sentences they can forward To know you're growing Talk about goals and ask for feedback

docs.title: A simple agenda (send it the day before)
docs.text:
1:1 agenda — [Date]
1. Wins this week: shipped X, fixed Y
2. In progress / risks: Z is at risk because…
3. Need from you: decision on A / intro to team B
4. Growth: feedback on my design review?

The 1:1 belongs to you

Don't let it turn into another status meeting. Keep 10 minutes for growth, feedback, and career.

docs.title: Scripts for common situations
docs.text:
Giving a status updateAsking for helpRaising a risk / delayPushing back on a deadlineAdmitting a mistakeAsking for feedbackAsking for a promotion / raiseDisagreeing with a decision

"Quick update on the payments API: on track for Friday. Endpoints are done, tests are 80% done. One risk: we're still waiting on the bank sandbox credentials. If they don't arrive by Wednesday, we slip a day. I've followed up with their team."

"I've been stuck on the Kafka consumer lag for about 4 hours. I've tried increasing partitions and tuning the batch size. Could you suggest someone who's worked on this, or spare 15 minutes?"

The 2-hour rule (beginners)

Struggle alone for up to ~2 hours, then ask, with what you tried. Asking too late costs more than asking too early.

"I want to flag a risk early. The search feature may slip by about 1 week. The OpenSearch mapping needs a reindex we didn't plan for. Two options: A) Ship on time without fuzzy search, add it next sprint. B) Keep full scope, ship next Friday. I'd recommend A. Which would you prefer?"

"I want to hit this date, so let me be realistic about it. With the current scope, my estimate is 3 weeks, not 2. To make 2 weeks, we could drop the export feature, or add one more developer for the UI. What matters most for this release?"

"I made a mistake: my migration yesterday dropped an index, and that's why the reports were slow. I've already restored it and reports are back to normal. To prevent it happening again, I'm adding a migration check to CI. Sorry for the trouble."

"I'm working on my communication. What's one thing I could do differently in design reviews?"

"I'd like to talk about my growth. Over the last year I led the checkout migration, cut deploy time by 80%, and mentored two new joiners. I believe I'm working at the senior level, and I'd like to be considered for promotion this cycle. What gaps do you see, and what would make the case clear?"

Tip

Bring your wins file with numbers. Ask for the gaps in writing. Agree on a timeline.

"Can I share a concern before we commit? Building our own auth will take 6–8 weeks and gives us security risk. Keycloak gets us 90% of it in a week. If you still prefer custom, I'll commit to it fully — I just want to make sure we've weighed this."

This is disagree and commit: voice it once, clearly, then support the decision.

docs.title: Mistakes to avoid
docs.text:
• ❌ Hiding bad news until the deadline
  • ❌ "It's almost done" for 3 weeks running (give percentages or remaining tasks instead)
  • ❌ Complaining about teammates without a suggestion
  • ❌ Treating every 1:1 as a status report
  • ❌ Waiting for your manager to bring up your career

docs.title: Beginner vs experienced
docs.text:
BeginnerExperienced
  • Over-communicate status. Silence makes people worry.
  • Write down what your manager asks so you don't have to ask twice.
  • Before a 1:1, prepare: 1 win, 1 blocker, 1 question.
  • Manage up: learn your manager's goals and pressures, and help them succeed.
  • Bring proposals, not just problems: "I'd like to own the reliability roadmap."
  • Give your manager feedback too: "It would help me if decisions came with the 'why'."

docs.title: Practice conversation: Raising a risk early
docs.text: YouDo you have five minutes? I want to flag a risk early. ManagerSure, go ahead. YouThe search feature may slip by a week. We need a full reindex that we didn't plan for. ManagerHmm. What are our options? YouOption A: we release on time without fuzzy search and add it next sprint. Option B: we release the full feature a week later. I'd recommend A. ManagerI agree with A. Can you update the product team? YouYes, I'll message them today and copy you.

docs.title: Day 66 · Team Building
docs.text: Day66Phase 4 · Workplace · Day 66 of 80 Done

docs.title: Team Building
docs.text: A team is built through small, repeated moments, not offsite games: how people greet each other, how mistakes are handled, who gets credit, and whether it's safe to say "I don't know". Everyone helps build it, not only the lead.

docs.title: What makes a strong team
docs.text:
1. Psychological safety — people can ask, admit mistakes and disagree without fear 2. Dependability — people do what they said, on time 3. Clarity — everyone knows the goals, roles and how decisions are made 4. Meaning — the work matters to the people doing it 5. Impact — people can see their work makes a difference

These come from widely cited research on what effective teams have in common. Psychological safety is the foundation the rest depend on.

docs.title: As a team member: what you can do
docs.text:
• Help first

    Review PRs quickly, answer questions in channels, pair with someone who's stuck.

  • Admit mistakes

    "That bug was mine. Here's the fix." When one person does this, others feel safe to do it too.

  • Give credit

    Thank people by name, publicly, for specific work.

  • Include people

    Invite the new joiner to lunch. Ask the quiet person for their view.

docs.title: As a team lead: building the team
Set it up clearly
docs.text:
Team charter (first team meeting)Opening scriptRoles & ownership

Agree these together and write them down:

## Our team charter
**Mission:** Make checkout fast and reliable for every customer.
**How we work:**
- Core hours 11–5 IST; async outside that
- PRs reviewed within 1 working day
- Disagree in the room, commit outside it
- Blameless post-mortems
**How we decide:** Owner decides after consulting; lead breaks ties
**How we communicate:** Slack for quick, docs for decisions, call for conflict

"I'd like us to agree on how we want to work together, not rules from me. What's one thing from a past team that worked really well, and one thing you never want to see again?"

Give everyone one clear area to own (a service, a process, the on-call runbook). Ownership builds commitment faster than any activity.

docs.title: Build psychological safety
docs.text: Do Say Model not knowing "I don't know. Who's worked with this before?" Thank people for bad news "Thanks for flagging this early. That's exactly what I want." Invite dissent "What are we missing? Who sees it differently?" Speak last in discussions (Let others share first so you don't anchor them) Handle mistakes as learning "What in our process allowed this? How do we fix the process?" Shut down disrespect quickly "Let's keep it about the idea, not the person."

docs.title: Rituals that build the team (low effort, high value)
docs.text: Ritual How Why it works Weekly wins 5 min on Friday: everyone shares one win Visibility + celebration Kudos channel #kudos for public thanks Recognition, especially across teams Demo day Monthly; anyone shows anything they built Pride, learning, cross-pollination Retro Every sprint; act on 1–2 items People see their input changes things Pairing / mob sessions 1–2 hours a week Knowledge sharing, relationships Lunch & learn Rotating speaker, 30 min Everyone teaches, everyone grows Onboarding buddy Each new joiner gets a buddy for 30 days Fast integration, a friend from day 1 Team lunch / chai Monthly, no work talk Personal connection

docs.title: Team activities
docs.text:
In-office / offsiteRemote / hybridIcebreakers that aren't awkward
  • Hackathon day: small mixed teams, a fun or useful problem, a demo at the end
  • Cooking / cricket / bowling outing: shared fun, without forced "trust falls"
  • Volunteering day: builds shared meaning
  • Strategy offsite: half the day on the team's direction, half on fun
  • Virtual coffee roulette: random pairs, 15 minutes, every week
  • Online games: quizzes, Pictionary-style drawing games, coding puzzles
  • "Show your desk / pet / hometown" in 2 minutes at the start of a meeting
  • Async photo channel: weekend pictures, food, travel
  • In-person meetup once or twice a year if possible
  • "What's one thing you're looking forward to this month?"
  • "What was your first ever computer or phone?"
  • "Best bug you've ever found or caused?"
  • "One app you couldn't live without?"
  • "What did you want to be when you were 10?"

Make activities inclusive

Not everyone drinks, eats every food, can stay late, or enjoys physical games. Mix the timings (some during work hours), the formats and the venues, and never make fun activities compulsory.

docs.title: Handling team problems
docs.text: Problem What to say / do Two people in conflict Meet each one privately, then together: "You both want the release to succeed. Let's agree how you'll work together." Silos ("my code, your code") Rotate code reviews and on-call; pair across areas One person carrying the team Share their knowledge (docs, pairing) and spread the load before they burn out Low morale after a hard period Acknowledge it honestly: "The last two months were tough." Celebrate what was achieved; give real rest New joiner not fitting in Assign a buddy, involve them in pairing, check in privately every week Cliques forming Mix pairs and project groups on purpose; include everyone in decisions

docs.title: Celebrating the team
docs.text:
"Before we close: thank you, everyone. We shipped slot booking in 3 cities with zero downtime. Special shout-out to Kavya for the load testing that caught the race condition, and to Arun for staying calm through two incidents. Lunch is on me on Friday!"

Be specific, name the people, and celebrate effort and learning, not only outcomes.

docs.title: Signs your team is healthy
docs.text:
• People ask "stupid" questions in public channels
  • Bad news reaches the lead early
  • Disagreements happen openly in meetings, not in private complaints afterwards
  • People help each other without being asked
  • Retro actions actually get done
  • People laugh together at least once a week

docs.title: Practice conversation: Setting up a team charter
docs.text: LeadI'd like us to agree on how we work together. What worked well in your past teams? KavyaFast code reviews. It's frustrating waiting three days. ArunBlameless post-mortems. In my last team, people hid mistakes. YouClear decisions. Sometimes we discuss for weeks and nobody decides. LeadGreat points. So: reviews within one working day, blameless post-mortems, and the owner decides after consulting? YouYes. And maybe a short "weekly wins" on Fridays? LeadLove it. I'll write it up and share it today.

docs.title: Day 58 · Team Lead Meetings
docs.text: Day58Phase 4 · Workplace · Day 58 of 80 Done

docs.title: Team Lead Meetings
docs.text:
Two sides of the same table. If you report to a team lead, this page shows how to use your time with them well. If you are the team lead, it shows how to run 1:1s, stand-ups, sprint planning and retros that people find useful rather than tiring.

Meeting your team lead Running meetings as a team lead

docs.title: What your team lead needs from you
docs.text: They need You give Visibility Short, regular status, before they ask Early risks "This might slip" on day 2, not day 10 Technical judgement Options and trade-offs, not just "it's hard" Ownership "I'll handle it" and follow-through Honest feedback What's working and what isn't in the team

docs.title: Your 1:1 with the team lead
docs.text:
1:1 — Team lead — [Date]
1. Progress: search filters done; sorting 70%
2. Blocker: need decision on pagination (cursor vs offset)
3. Tech question: should we cache category tree in Redis?
4. Growth: can I lead the next design review?
5. Team: onboarding docs are outdated — happy to fix

docs.title: Scripts
docs.text:
Getting a technical decisionAsking for more responsibilityToo much workGiving feedback to your leadConcern about a teammate

"I need a decision on pagination. Option A: offset, which is simple but slow past page 100. Option B: cursor, which is fast but can't jump to an arbitrary page. Product says users rarely go past page 5, so I recommend cursor. Okay to go ahead?"

"I'd like to grow toward a senior role. Could I own the delivery-slot service end to end, from design to on-call? I'd check in with you on the design before building."

"I have the search work, two production bugs and the interview loop this week. I can't do all of it well. Which should I drop or push to next week?"

"Can I share some feedback? When requirements change mid-sprint, it'd help to know the reason. Last week the team rewrote the cart API twice without context, and people felt frustrated. A quick note on the 'why' would make a big difference."

"I want to raise something carefully. I've noticed the integration tests have been skipped on the last few PRs, and it caused yesterday's staging break. I've mentioned it to Arun directly. Could we talk about a team-wide rule so it doesn't feel personal?"

Talk to the person first. Escalate the pattern, not the person.

docs.title: Mistakes to avoid
docs.text:
• ❌ Showing up to the 1:1 with nothing to discuss
  • ❌ Bringing problems without any proposed solution
  • ❌ Agreeing in the meeting and complaining after it
  • ❌ Using the 1:1 only for status (that's what stand-up is for)

docs.title: The meeting toolkit
docs.text: Meeting Frequency Length Goal Daily stand-up Daily 15 min Sync & unblock 1:1 Weekly / bi-weekly 30 min Trust, growth, early warnings Sprint planning Every sprint 60–90 min Commit to realistic scope Backlog refinement Weekly 45 min Clarify & estimate upcoming work Retrospective Every sprint 45–60 min Improve how we work Tech / design review As needed 45 min Make good technical decisions together

docs.title: 1:1s with your team members
docs.text:
Their meeting, not yours. Let them set most of the agenda; you listen 70% of the time.

Great 1:1 questions:

  • "What's on your mind this week?"
  • "What's blocking you or slowing you down?"
  • "What's one thing I could do to make your work easier?"
  • "What are you enjoying most right now? Least?"
  • "Where do you want to be in a year? What could get you there?"
  • "Is there anything in the team that bothers you that I might not see?"

Never cancel 1:1s

Reschedule if you must. Cancelling repeatedly tells people they're not a priority.

docs.title: Stand-up: keep it tight
docs.text:
"Morning, everyone! Same format: done, doing, blockers. Let's keep detailed discussions for after. Kavya, want to start?"

Redirect long discussions: "Great point. Ravi and Meena, can you two take that right after?"

docs.title: Sprint planning
docs.text:
"Our sprint goal: launch delivery-slot booking in Pune. Last 3 sprints we averaged 34 points, and 2 people are on leave, so let's commit to about 26. Anything that doesn't serve the goal goes to the stretch list."

  • Start with the goal, then pick stories
  • Plan around real capacity (leave, on-call, interviews)
  • Make sure every story has clear acceptance criteria
  • Ask the quiet people: "Arun, does that estimate feel right to you?"

docs.title: Retrospectives that actually change things
docs.text:
Format: Start / Stop / Continue (or Went well / Didn't go well / Ideas)

"The goal is to improve the system, not to blame anyone. What happens in the retro is safe to say here. Let's take 5 minutes to write silently, then share."

  • Pick at most 2 action items, each with an owner
  • Start the next retro by reviewing last retro's actions
  • Rotate the facilitator so everyone gets a turn

docs.title: Design reviews
docs.text:
• Ask the author to share the doc 24 hours before
  • Speak last as the lead, so you don't anchor the room
  • Ask: "What alternatives did we consider? What's the riskiest part? How do we roll back?"
  • End with a decision, or with exactly what's needed to make one

docs.title: Handling team dynamics in meetings
docs.text: Situation What to say One person dominates "Thanks, Rahul. Let's hear from someone who hasn't spoken yet. Priya?" Someone stays silent (Later, 1:1) "I'd love to hear your view in meetings. Would it help if I asked you directly?" Two people argue "You both have valid points. Let's write down the trade-offs and decide with data." Meeting going off-topic "Let's park that. I'll add it to the next refinement." Blame starts "Let's focus on what in the process allowed this, not who." Bad news for the team "I'll be straight with you: the deadline moved up 2 weeks. Here's what I know and what I'm pushing back on."

docs.title: Communicating up and down
docs.text: To the team To your manager / leadership Context: why we're doing this Outcomes, risks, decisions needed Shield from noise and churn Advocate for the team's capacity Credit individuals publicly Report problems with your plan to fix them Be honest about uncertainty Escalate early with options

docs.title: New team lead: first 30 days
docs.text:
• 1:1 with every team member: "What should I keep? What should I change?"
  • Learn the current processes before changing any
  • Meet key stakeholders (PM, QA, other leads)
  • Agree on expectations with your manager
  • Fix one small irritation quickly to build trust
  • Shift from "I did" to "we did". Your success is now the team's success.

docs.title: Practice conversation: Asking your team lead for a decision
docs.text: YouI need a quick decision on pagination for the search API. LeadOkay, what are the options? YouOffset pagination is simple but slow after page 100. Cursor pagination is fast but users can't jump to a page number. LeadWhat do users actually do? YouProduct data says 98% never go past page 5. So I recommend cursor. LeadMakes sense. Go with cursor, and note the decision in the design doc. YouWill do. Thanks.
